EntertainmentTab.title: Girl group Katseye are missing two members, but their tour still dazzles
EntertainmentTab.text:
They may have been two members down, but the pop group Katseye received a hero's welcome as they played their first full concert in the UK.

The audience erupted with screams even before the show began, as the band broadcast their music videos on the O2 Arena's big screens, and the noise barely dipped for the next three hours.

It was proof that Katseye have become pop's biggest property (they're currently the most-streamed act on YouTube UK) even while singers Manon Bannerman and Sophia Laforteza are on health-related hiatus.

The stage felt emptier without them, but their bandmates worked hard to fill the gaps, hyping up the crowd with a succession of bass-heavy pop anthems and jaw-dropping dance breaks.

"Are you happy to see us?" asked the band's youngest member, Yoonchae Jeong, as if the answer hadn't been obvious from the moment they appeared in a storm of laser lights and launched into the Brazilian funk workout of Hootie Frutti.

"I think you guys are our loudest crowd ever, literally," marvelled Megan Skiendiel.

"This crowd is unbelievable," added Lara Raj.

The concert was only the second date of the band's Wildworld tour - but fans already knew every twist and turn from social media.

There was even a cheer of relief when Daniela Avanzini survived a complicated lift in the dance routine for Gabriella. On the opening night, her dance partner dropped her., external

Such adulation - and scrutiny - has come quickly for Katseye.

Based in Los Angeles, the multinational girl group were only formed in 2023 as part of the online reality competition show The Debut: Dream Academy.

The contest was created by Hybe, the South Korean entertainment company behind acts like BTS and Le Sserafim, and the US record label Geffen, home to Olivia Rodrigo and the Rolling Stones. Of the 120,000 who initially applied for the show, only six made it through.

Trained under the rigorous K-Pop system, they had a breakout year in 2025, first with the hyperactive electro-skronk of their single Gnarly, then with its follow-up, a slinky ballad called Gabriela that highlighted Daniela's Cuban-Venezuelan roots.

In London, their audience skewed young: The queue for pick and mix was longer than the one for the bar.

When Megan asked, "Whose first concert is this?" the air curdled with screams.

Throughout the show, fans shook lightsticks, parroted Katseye's dance moves and, in some cases, spontaneously burst into tears.

Many concert-goers also wore bindis, inspired by Lara, who has proudly incorporated her Asian heritage into her aesthetic.

One individual also came dressed as a courgette, a reference to Internet Girl's so-weird-it-almost-works refrain, "Eat zucchini".

The energy was infectious. And, if you looked closely, the parents were enjoying the show as much as their kids.

Even Spice Girl Melanie C is a fan, hosting a Q&A with the band during their first UK trip last October.

"They're incredible girls," she told the BBC earlier this summer. "They've got great music, they've got a great work ethic, and they're really beautiful, you know?

"Obviously, they've had a little drama, as happens with all bands, but they work so goddamn hard."

The drama began in February, when Manon announced she was taking a hiatus from the band to "focus on her health and wellbeing".

It came after the Swiss-Ghanaian singer told BBC News the band had been subject to racism and death threats; but fans also highlighted Katseye's gruelling schedule, suggesting they were being overworked.

In April, she posted a message to fans saying she was having "positive conversations" with Katseye's management, but not before she removed references to the band from her Instagram biography.

Then, just months after Manon stepped back, Sophia announced she was also going on hiatus to protect her "mental health and wellness".

"You can't pour from an empty cup," she posted on social media. "It's important to care for yourself."

Which brings me to a related point. After the tour's opened in Dublin on Tuesday, Katseye were accused of miming throughout their set.

But from what I could tell on Thursday, the member's microphones were live all night, with a backing track doubling their vocals at crucial moments.

On slower songs like Tonight I Might and My Way they proved more than capable as live performers.

Meanwhile, Lara's vocals on the solo showcase unloveu (proudly introduced as "the first Katseye song written by a member of Katseye") mixed power and emotion in a way that suggested the band have potential beyond the ear candy pop that's become their trademark.

Other highlights included Daniela's death-defying dance break, complete with aerial splits, that led into Gabriella; and Megan's technotronic shakedown at the end of Pinky Up.

For Yoonchae, the show's high point was Time Lapse, where she got to sing in her native Korean, while mingling with the crowd. ("Keep your hands to yourselves and don't throw any gifts on the stage for our safety," warned Lara, spoiling the atmosphere just a little).

The show ended on a powerful note, with Iconic By Mistake - the band's defiant response to an online hate campaign - and an extended romp through Gnarly, complete with a leather-studded rock remix.

All told, it was a stunningly confident and self-assured show from a band who could easily been diminished by personnel problems.

"This is not a goodbye," promised Yooncahe as Katseye waved goodbye. "We'll come back."

Glastonbury's Pyramid Stage would be a perfect fit.

EntertainmentTab.title: Rob Brydon 'regrets' turning down Dolly Parton interview
EntertainmentTab.text:
Gavin and Stacey star Rob Brydon says he "regrets" turning down the chance to interview Dolly Parton after choosing to stay on a family holiday.

Brydon fronted the BBC documentary series Honky Tonk Road Trip, where he travelled across the American South to celebrate 100 years of country music.

In it he visited Dollywood, a theme park created by Parton, where Dolly's relatives had traced the lineage of the Parton and Owens sides to Wales.

He was told he could interview Parton if he returned after filming had ended, but chose to stay on his family holiday in Arizona - an opportunity he now wished he had taken because he never got to meet her before she died.

Parton died peacefully in hospital in Nashville on 25 August following a brief battle with cancer. She was admitted to hospital four days before her death with kidney and autoimmune issues.

"I sort of regret it now," he told Lucy Owen during an interview on BBC Radio Wales.

"I kind of wish that I had gone back because I never met her."

The Welsh actor and comedian's debut children's book - The Cat in The Cupboard - will be published on 10 September.

Aimed at children aged between five and seven, the tale was inspired by the stories he invented for his children about their own ginger cat.

Brydon said he had long made up stories and songs "for my own enjoyment" and was excited to share this with others.

The story, which is told entirely in rhyme, follows Crumble the cat on his daring garden adventures.

He explained the idea came when they had to move their cat flap and "it went to the corner of the house... which meant that he came into the house via a cupboard".

"I just remember saying, 'Oh, the cat in the cupboard, the cat in the cupboard, that sounds nice'," he said.

Brydon also spoke about another writing duo he admires - his fellow Gavin and Stacey cast mates Ruth Jones and James Corden.

He shared that he "can't wait" to see their new comedy project, The Choir, adding: "They have a kind of magic when they write together."

But said he doesn't "know if any of our crowd are in it".

However, he told eager listeners that the cast are "still very much in touch" via their "active WhatsApp group".

"It was Alison's birthday the other day and there was a flurry of activity then," he said.

EntertainmentTab.title: 'Not only did I survive, I thrived' - Meera Syal after assaults
EntertainmentTab.text:
Dame Meera Syal has said she "almost gave up" her career after being sexually harassed and assaulted by two "predators" within the media industry.

"I was out of work, I was homeless, sleeping on people's floors, and then these two things happened in quite quick succession," the Wolverhampton-born star said in a candid interview with BBC Asian Network's Amber Haque.

In her new memoir, Vigilauntie, which was published on Thursday, the actress shared that both incidents happened in her 20s, as she was struggling to secure a role.

Now aged 65, she has opened up about the harrowing experiences and reflected on how she overcame them to become one of the most well-known faces on British TV.

"It could have been a point where I gave up," she explained.

"It put some fire in my belly because the reason I wanted to tell these stories is that I did survive, and not only did I survive, I thrived.

"The anger of the injustice of the situation made me seek out a bunch of women that changed the course of my life."

Syal described the first incident as "my first casting couch approach".

She wrote that the man, a theatre director, insinuated he would give her a role in a pantomime if she engaged in sexual acts with him. She refused and was able to leave.

However, a few weeks later an older male actor invited her to his home under the guise that he would help her progress with her career. Instead he assaulted her, she wrote in her book.

The predatory actor has since died.

The comedy star, known for shows including Goodness Gracious Me and The Kumars at No 42, did not report the incidents to the police and did not tell family or friends as it "was the culture" of the industry at the time.

She recalled: "When I have talked about this incident to other women, particularly of my age, they've all said that happened to me and a lot of them have never talked about it because it was part of the culture.

"The 70s, 80s and 90s, it was absolutely part of the culture.

"You wouldn't even bother to report half of these things because A, you wouldn't be believed and B, everyone was doing it."

Joining the BBC in the 1990s, she rose to prominence as part of the team behind the broadcaster's sketch comedy, Goodness Gracious Me!

In 1993, she wrote the screenplay for the comedy-drama film Bhaji On The Beach, and two years later she starred in the Channel 4 romantic comedy film, Beautiful Thing.

The award-winner was a key writer and actress on the 1996 show, and later helped to bring Bollywood to the West End, by co-writing Andrew Lloyd Webber's Bombay Dreams in 2002.

You can listen to the full interview with Dame Meera Syal on Asian Network Trending on BBC Sounds.

If you've been affected by the issues in this story, help and support is available via the BBC Action Line.

EntertainmentTab.title: How Oasis fans cracked the Celtic Park gigs code in chip shop video
EntertainmentTab.text:
Oasis fans have uncovered a set of cryptic clues in a promo video from the band, suggesting that they will stage gigs at Celtic Park in Glasgow next year.

The Manchester rockers released the 23-second teaser on their social media accounts, showing two boys in what appears to be a Scottish chip shop.

Internet sleuths spotted sets of numbers in posters around the chippy which they worked out to be the map co-ordinates for Celtic's Parkhead stadium.

It has fuelled speculation that the band will be playing at the venue next year- possibly as the first date of a new tour.

It follows the Gallagher brothers' hugely successful reunion tour which saw them perform at 41 sold-out stadium shows in 14 countries.

This included three dates at Murrayfield Stadium, Edinburgh, in August 2025, when they played to 200,000 fans.

The clues hinting at a Celtic Park gig include an advert for a £55.84 family chippy bundle and a poster for radio station Sol FM 98 92.

The numbers spell out the 55.849892N latitude of the stadium.

There is also a sticker on the fridge saying it should be kept at -4, a poster saying the daily special is priced at £2.05 and a taxi number featuring the area code 638.

These numbers together are -4.205638W - Celtic Park's longitude.

Other Scottish clues include the actor Robert Carlyle, who features in the video for Oasis song Little by Little which plays on a TV in the background.

The chip shop fridge is filled with Irn Bru and other AG Barr brands.

One of the boys also hands over a Mars Bar to be deep fried - a Scottish chippy delicacy.

Fans have also posted theories about other "clues" on social media.

One said the position of the two boys is similar to the positions of Noel and Liam Gallagher on the front of the Definitely Maybe album, with the fridge being in a similar position to the window.

Celtic Park has not hosted any concerts for a number of years with the last being Wet, Wet Wet in 1997.

Other noteable gigs there have been Rod Stewart, Status Quo and Joe Cocker in 1991, Bryan Adams and Prince in 1992, U2 and Utah Saints in 1993.

Rod Stewart performed there again in 2014 during the Opening Ceremony for the Commonwealth Games.

Glasgow's Hampden Park has become the city's main concert stadium over the past three decades.

EntertainmentTab.title: Freddie Mercury mural unveiled at Wembley for 80th birthday
EntertainmentTab.text:
A 30ft (9m) mural of Freddie Mercury has been unveiled at Wembley Park to mark what would have been the singer's 80th birthday.

The artwork, called I'm Mr Mercury, is anamorphic, meaning the image only resolves when viewed from a single marked spot about 65ft away. From anywhere else it breaks up into colour and line.

It was created by the street artist Frank Styles, who hand-sprayed it as four separate works before composing them into a single image across all 58 of the site's Spanish Steps.

Mercury, born on 5 September 1946, performed at Wembley repeatedly with Queen.

The band played 10 shows at the venue, previously known as the Empire Pool, between 1978 and 1984, and appeared at Live Aid at Wembley Stadium in July 1985. Queen returned to the stadium for two sold-out concerts the following summer.

The mural also refers to Mercury's life away from the stage. Koi carp reflect his love of Japan and the Japanese pond at his London home, while winged female figures echo his Virgo star sign, a motif he used on the Queen crest he designed himself.

Lyrics and quotations run up the steps towards the stadium.

Claudio Giambrone, who commissioned and curated the work for Wembley Park, said: "Freddie Mercury's relationship with Wembley goes far beyond a single famous performance.

"We wanted to create something that gives fans a new place in Wembley where they can come together and remember him."

Styles said: "As a trained graphic designer himself, Freddie was very aware and precise about the visual feel and so I have endeavoured to follow his ethos in the conscious creation of this mural."

The steps link Wembley Stadium and the OVO Arena, formerly Wembley Arena. The mural is free to view at any time and will remain in place until December 2026.

EntertainmentTab.title: Aardman at 50: Gromit was nearly a cat, Shaun the Sheep almost spoke
EntertainmentTab.text:
Gromit was almost a cat. Shaun the Sheep was nearly given a voice. And Chicken Run helped change the Oscars forever.

As Aardman Animations marks its 50th birthday, its creators have been sharing some of the surprising twists behind the rise of Bristol's best-known creative success story.

Founded by school friends Sir Peter Lord and Sir David Sproxton in 1976, Aardman has given us Morph, Wallace and Gromit, Shaun the Sheep and Chicken Run, the world's most successful stop-motion film.

But the journey from two teenagers "mucking about with plasticine" to an Oscar-winning animation powerhouse has often hinged on chance decisions, practical compromises and creative instinct.

Few examples are better than Gromit.

Wallace and Gromit became Aardman's most famous characters after animator Nick Park joined the studio in 1985.

But Gromit was not always a dog.

"I had this idea of an English guy who builds a rocket, in the basement of his house," recalled Park.

"I was thinking he may have a pet, probably a cat."

The switch was surprisingly simple.

"I started modelling the cat, and it was just very difficult, so I thought I'd do a dog instead!"

Park was developing A Grand Day Out at the National Film and Television School in London when Lord and Sproxton came to speak to students.

"We met him and thought, 'Oh, he's good'. In fact, he's very good. Now I know him, he's actually a genius," said Lord.

The combination was electric. A Grand Day Out was nominated for an Oscar in 1990, losing only to another Aardman production, Creature Comforts, also directed by Park.

Pointing to a poster of Wallace and Gromit floating over Bristol in a hot-air balloon, Lord reflected on their appeal.

"When they appear on the screen, you laugh before they do anything."

Park later won three more Oscars. Perhaps it was just as well he never mastered Gromit the Cat.

By the mid-1990s, Wallace and Gromit had made Aardman one of the most talked-about names in animation.

That success led to an unlikely meeting with Steven Spielberg.

At dinner with Spielberg and DreamWorks chief executive Jeffrey Katzenberg, they pitched what became Chicken Run.

"We want to do The Great Escape," Lord told Spielberg.

"But with chickens."

"I had always been a fan of Aardman," Katzenberg said. "And I had this secret ambition that someday there would be a way to work together."

Park remembered Spielberg's response.

"Spielberg said, 'The Great Escape is one of my favourite films, and I have 300 chickens on my ranch!' So it went very well."

No-one had ever made a 90-minute stop-motion feature from modelling clay. The budget was more than £20m, and Aardman insisted every frame would be shot in Bristol.

The gamble paid off. Chicken Run took more than $220m (£165m) worldwide and remains the highest-grossing stop-motion film ever made.

But it did not win an Oscar.

At the time there was no Academy Award for animated features.

"And so because they couldn't give Chicken Run a little golden man, they invented the category," said Radio 1 film critic Ali Plumb.

The Academy introduced the Best Animated Feature Oscar the following year.

"And a couple of years later, Wallace and Gromit won that Oscar for 'The Curse of the Were-Rabbit', so they got their own reward," Plumb said.

If Chicken Run proved Aardman could conquer Hollywood, another character would go on to conquer the world.

Shaun first appeared in the Wallace and Gromit film A Close Shave in 1995 and has become one of the studio's biggest global stars.

Like all the other animals, he expresses himself through bleats, grunts and hugely dynamic facial expressions.

"The beauty of Shaun is it transcends borders and cultures because it doesn't rely on the spoken word," said Aardman's Managing Director Sean Clarke.

"You can literally see Shaun the Sheep here in Bristol and in Outer Mongolia."

Yet executives repeatedly urged Aardman to give him a voice.

"When we launched the Shaun the Sheep series, we were told to add voices," Clarke remembered.

The same argument resurfaced when Shaun got his own feature film in 2015.

"They said, 'You can't do 80 minutes without any dialogue'.

"But we stuck to our convictions, and I think it is now one of our most revered films."

Lord insists Shaun was not kept silent to boost international sales, it simply "seemed better that way".

However, the character's global appeal is undeniable. Clarke said Shaun has been sold into 170 countries and is especially popular in Asia.

"Shaun is actually our most valuable character now.

"Wallace and Gromit built the house, but Shaun keeps the lights on."

If that cheque gave them a company name, their next creation gave them a star.

Lord and Sproxton moved to Bristol to work on Take Hart, the successor to Vision On.

On this show they took what Lord called "a leap into the third dimension".

"Plasticine was cheap", Lord explained.

"The budgets were low, and you can work quickly with it."

Soon he had fashioned Morph, the simple little terracotta brown figure that can change shape into anything, hence his name.

"It was just so easy to squash him up and reform him as a dog, or a submarine, or a bird or anything," Lord said.

Morph became a hit with children and parents alike, and remains a fixture at Aardman's Bristol headquarters.

Back in 1989, Lord told a BBC West documentary The Animators he "hoped Morph will still be around in 30 years or so, and still be loved."

It has been 37 years since he said that, and an Aardman exhibition at Bristol's MShed Museum was recently packed with Morph superfans.

But Lord, now the studio's creative director, still comes into the office and playfully reshapes Morph while chatting.

I asked him what Wallace would make of it all.

"Oh, he'd probably just say 'Cracking careers lads!'" he smiled.

As Aardman Animations marks its 50th birthday, its creators have been sharing some of the surprising twists behind the rise of Bristol's best-known creative success story. Founded by school friends...

EntertainmentTab.title: Why Northern Ireland was the 'perfect place' for The Death of Robin Hood
EntertainmentTab.text:
It is a centuries old legend of stealing from the rich to give to the poor, freshly adapted for the big screen, filmed entirely in Northern Ireland.

The Death of Robin Hood is based on a 17th Century ballad of the outlaw, starring Hugh Jackman as the reflective, battle-weary titular character at the end of his life. It presents a darker, less family-friendly version of the medieval hero.

A Belfast actress, who played a small role in the film, told BBC News NI about sharing the screen with A-listers and why Northern Ireland was now "the perfect place" to make a film.

Tabitha Smyth, from the east of the city, was cast as Sarah in her first role in a major studio feature film.

"The film's set in England, but Northern Ireland is just like the perfect place to film for everyone at the minute - you can get from a beach to a city centre, to a forest park, all within 20 minutes of each other," Smyth said.

"It's like a dream for a production like this, where it is set hundreds of years ago, hence why Game of Thrones and stuff like How to Train Your Dragon etc have all been filmed in the north."

Filming spanned across a wide range of picturesque parts of the country including Silent Valley, Glenarm and Murlough Bay.

Production was also based at Belfast Harbour Studios, whilst the film's post-production process was completed at the company Yellow Moon in Holywood.

The film has a small cast but some big names - Jodie Comer, Bill Skarsgård and Noah Jupe.

Smyth said it was "very daunting", but Comer and Jackman were "so down to earth"

"Obviously going into a film like that when you haven't been in a film before and then you're just like on set with like Jodie Comer and Hugh Jackman," she said.

"It was pretty much every scene or every part I was doing they were in there as well, which was kind of mad."

Strangford and Bushmills were also among the locations to provide a dramatic backdrop for the film.

"There were times where mad storms were happening, when they were filming, like it was kind of crazy, rain, hail and snow," Smyth said.

The actor said filming in Northern Ireland brought an authenticity to the film.

"We were filming a scene and it was absolutely freezing, like on the edge of a cliff. There was a fire lit and the wind was mad, but it just adds to it because it would have looked look like that," she said.

Northern Ireland is also popular with the crews, she added.

"The people are all really sound, the food's good, the craic is good and people are really drawn to it at the minute in producing work here," she said.

"Game of Thrones has a really big part to play in that for sure."

Andrew Reid, chief content officer at Northern Ireland Screen, told BBC News NI that productions like this have become a "regular occurrence" in Northern Ireland.

He said there had been a particular rise in the number of indigenous productions – that is, productions written, directed and produced in Northern Ireland.

Like Smyth, he believes Northern Ireland lends itself perfectly to film-making.

"We are a small but very compact region, it's easy to get around," Reid said.

"Time on the road is wasted money.

"We can be up a mountain in the morning, and in a studio in the afternoon. There's a really good selection of diverse locations."

However, Reid said Northern Ireland had other star qualities for film-makers.

"We have a fantastic ecosystem that has been built up over decades," he said. "We have fantastic people.

"We also have a very strong training remit within our productions that we're building up those crews."

Reid added that the region's "state-of-the-art facilities" were also a major draw.

So how long until Northern Ireland can call itself a major player in European film?

According to Reid, the talent, facilities and landscape of the area mean it might be sooner than some expect.

"We're starting to see the beginning of it already."

The Death of Robin Hood was released in the UK on 2 September.

EntertainmentTab.title: Carla Jeffery: 'Beautiful, vibrant' Disney star dies aged 33
EntertainmentTab.text:
US actress Carla Jeffery, who was known for appearing in 2018 Disney Channel movie Zombies and two sequels, has died at the age of 33.

Announcing the news, her agent Carla Alexander described her as a "beautiful, vibrant and incredibly talented woman whose radiant smile could light up any room".

Jeffery played cheerleader Bree in Zombies and its follow-ups in 2020 and 2022, and previously had a recurring role in Curb Your Enthusiasm as one of the Black family, who moved in with Larry David after Hurricane Katrina.

No cause of death has been given.

Her management company Alexanders Talent wrote on Instagram, external: "Our hearts are broken as we mourn the loss of our beloved Carla Jeffery.

"For more than 20 years, Carla was part of the Alexanders Talent Management family and watching her grow from a talented young girl into the beautiful, vibrant woman and actress she became was an incredible privilege.

"We will remember her infectious smile, her laughter, her talent, and the beautiful light she carried everywhere she went.

"Our deepest love and condolences are with Carla's family and loved ones. We ask that their privacy be respected during this incredibly difficult time. Rest beautifully, Carla. You will be deeply missed and forever loved."

Jeffery's twin brother Carlon, who is also an actor, reposted that statement as well as a clip of his sister on a beach and a screenshot of an undated text message.

"Hey Sis, call me back when you get this. I was just calling to see how your day went! I love you to the moon & back sis," it read.

"I just want you to know how proud I am of you. Your resilience, your grace, your infectious smile that lights up a room. You are truly a light that shines bright. Don't let anyone dim that light, even yourself.

"The light you carry is special and must be protected at all times. You are the best sister a brother could ask for. Pray we continue to grow closer to one another along this journey. I got your back in this life and the next."

Her co-stars also paid tribute, with Chandler Kinney, who played Willa in Zombies, writing that the actress's death "doesn't feel real".

"Carla. The sweetest, most sparkly gal. You made every day better and brighter with your infectious positivity," Kinney wrote.

"I think part of why you brought such effervescence to Bree (aside from your immense talent) is because that's really who you were in your heart; a bubbly, vivacious heart-of-gold cheerleader who loved nothing more than to uplift those around her."

Milo Manheim, who played Zed, shared a series of photos with the caption: "Love you Carlaboo, the sweetest, kindest, most loving person."

GeneralTab.title: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' in foreign donor talks
GeneralTab.text:
Nigel Farage has said he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what appears to have been a scheme to funnel foreign money to Reform UK.

His former chief of staff Dan Jukes and ex-head of policy James Orr have both been removed from their jobs after an investigation recorded them talking about how to get money to the party from an American donor and asking a fake company to pay for polling.

Jukes has denied doing anything wrong. Orr has told Sky News he will co-operate fully with Reform's internal investigation.

In an interview with the BBC, the Reform leader said he was not listening to the discussion and revealed his family are "begging" him to leave his job amid increasing pressure.

In a film by Verbatim Investigations and Channel 4 News, Farage and Jukes were present during a conversation in which it is suggested the US donor gives £500,000 to Reform through his UK-based son.

Under electoral law, donors to UK political parties must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK, so cannot give money from abroad through a British resident.

The proposed donation was never made as it was part of an undercover sting, but that it was seemingly entertained has sparked questions.

When asked about the exchange by reporters at Reform's party conference on Friday, Farage said he was questioning whether the arrangement was above board.

In an interview to be broadcast on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, he has now said: "I am not a compliance officer. I was in the middle of canvassing in the Clacton by-election. I turn up. I frankly wasn't even listening."

"I was told there was a global family office based in London, so the money could have come from Singapore," he said of the conversation in the Channel 4 film.

"The money could come from all over the world, you know. Income could have came from all over the world into a family office based in London. I know electoral law. I know donation law better than anybody.

"Frankly, the two individuals involved here have never been involved in fundraising before and they shouldn't have been involved directly in fundraising. They should have done basic checks and nobody, nobody should be brought to me, unless they've been vetted from."

The row over the Channel 4 film has threatened to capsize Reform's conference, with Labour and the Liberal Democrats calling on the Metropolitan Police to investigate the claims. The force is assessing whether or not to investigate.

Jukes and Orr - both senior figures in Farage's inner circle - have stood down pending the outcome of the party's internal investigation, but political opponents are demanding that Farage is investigated and takes accountability.

Farage categorically denied that Reform had ever taken money from a foreign entity by channelling it through a UK donor.

But as pressure ramps up on Farage in the latest crisis to rock Reform, he also told the BBC that "for the first time", he does not have his family's support to be in politics.

"They would rather I packed it up and walked away," he said.

He added he had not considered standing down, but "when you've got your family begging you to, it's not easy".

Farage also condemned the hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters who descended on the Port of Dover on Saturday morning, causing major travel disruption.

Farage said he "deplored" anyone wearing masks or balaclavas at public demonstrations.

He added: "You should not be allowed to be masked up, balaclava-ed up and go out and protest on the streets of our country. It is wrong at every level. So I deplore what is happening in Dover today."

There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.

Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days".

They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats.

They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029.

They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest.

Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage.

But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.

What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.

At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake.

One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions".

No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty".

And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.

Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.

A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up – sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage".

Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said.

But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera – Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say."

But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"

This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing.

Farage's admission that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling – to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.

GeneralTab.title: Reform UK winded by donations row as insiders call for shift in approach
GeneralTab.text:
"We are still a bit of a pirate ship," a senior Reform figure acknowledges privately.

It was the recurring conversation throughout Reform UK's conference in Birmingham: the consequences of the undercover filming broadcast by Channel 4 News which has cost two senior party figures their jobs, at least for now.

How much damage does it cause to Reform? And what does it tell us about them?

"A key part of the appeal of us is the sense of us being cavaliers. Doing things differently. Standing out. And that's great. But we need roundheads too. Those who ask the boring questions. Do the checks. We need more of them too," this same senior figure adds.

The story of Reform over the last 12 months can be summarised in three words: defections, elections and money.

Defections, those who leave one party and join another, have been a big part of the party's growth in the last year – not least the recruitment of former Conservative cabinet ministers Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman.

Elections have been as well - Reform's gains in the English local elections and the devolved parliament elections in Wales and in Scotland.

But so too has money. The backdrop to this conference was the swirl of questions about money even before Channel 4 News', and Verbatim Investigations', endeavours.

In the hour or two before its broadcast on Thursday night, senior Reform figures, including those directly caught up in it, projected a sense of being relatively relaxed about it. Awkward, embarrassing, but survivable.

Once it was broadcast, things changed. There was fury, I am told, and very quickly there was a sense of its gravity. "A few bottles of red were had, and we knew we had to act," is how one source described it to me. The conversations went on into the early hours.

Firstly, there was anger that it would drown out a conference that has been months in the planning. And yes, it has dominated conversation here in Birmingham.

Secondly, there was widespread concern about the image it projected, the impression it would leave.

Reform wants to project itself as a prospective party of government.

And yet the headlines allow critics to claim they are not just ramshackle and amateurish but can point to what looks like a pattern of activity, consciously pursued, to breach the law.

Absolutely not, Nigel Farage insisted to me, there was no such pattern.

But what of the ethos of the party? Journalist Tim Shipman in The Spectator writes , externalthat "it is the experience of everyone I have ever known near the summit of politics that political operations take their character and operating logic from the person at the apex of the triangle. Leaders set culture."

There is something in this. Take Rishi Sunak's Downing Street operation and Boris Johnson's. They were wildly different culturally, reflecting the very different characters at their helm. Would all the things that happened during Partygate under Johnson have happened under Sunak? Unlikely, I would have thought.

Some within Reform, who are full of admiration for Nigel Farage's chutzpah and gift as a communicator, are desperate to see a behind-the-scenes cultural shift that minimises the chances of further embarrassments. And, alongside that, a step up in the infrastructure and personnel to match.

Farage's team express frustration that this is precisely what they have been doing, but some are telling them internally they need to move more quickly.

Both James Orr, the party's head of policy; and Dan Jukes, Farage's right-hand man, will be missed profoundly by those inside the party.

Privately, some wonder if Orr may yet return.

Jukes, who has been a pivotal and loyal figure in Team Farage for years, was already dividing his time between the UK and the United States as his wife and baby are on the other side of the Atlantic.

Perhaps, some senior figures suggest, his immediate future might be in America. Does he return when the general election is nearer? Let's see.

Reform leave Birmingham winded and wounded by the last few days, their days in the sun overshadowed.

The question is how they deal with this and respond to it, in the coming weeks and months.

GeneralTab.title: Cleveland police chief proud of force but being 'let down' by funding
GeneralTab.text:
Cleveland Police's Chief Constable has said she is proud of her "brave" force but that it was being "let down" by the way it was funded, following a fatal crash which killed seven people including two police officers.

In her first sit-down interview since the A66 crash, speaking exclusively to the BBC, Victoria Fuller said the force needed to become part of a larger force with greater resources.

She said her officers are dealing with some of the highest crime levels in the country akin to those faced by metropolitan forces, but with less than half the number of officers.

Multiple people have since been arrested as part of a wider police operation against organised crime following the crash.

A Volkswagen Passat carrying five young men drove the wrong way down the motorway near Middlesbrough in the early hours of the morning before colliding with a marked police car.

Officers had been pursuing the car for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when the Passat turned on to the dual carriageway, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said.

Fuller, whose force covers an area of north-east England that includes Middlesbrough and Teesside, recalled being asleep when the duty commander rang her with the news.

"No matter how tragic and devastated you feel, we swing into action and we do what we need to do," she said.

The home secretary announced this week that Cleveland Police would be given an extra £2m to deal with the fallout from the crash, with 200 officers drafted in from elsewhere.

Fuller told the BBC on Friday that she was grateful for the support the force had been given, but added: "I need that all the time."

Cleveland's Labour police and crime commissioner has previously said the force needed an extra £20m a year to hire more officers and crack down on organised crime.

Cleveland Police is grappling with the highest recorded crime rate of anywhere in England and Wales, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures for the year to March show.

It also ranks highest for burglary, sexual offences, violence with injury, and criminal damage and arson.

Fuller said Cleveland Police had also experienced the largest decrease in the number of officers since 2010 and was staffed as if it were a rural force.

"It absolutely needs to change," she said.

Fuller expressed hope that reform to policing across the country was on the horizon, and that Cleveland Police would become one of the "big, strategic forces that have the resource, the flex and the capability to surge when they need to surge".

She added: "In the meantime, we need additional funding... to take us to that point."

Recent inspections show Cleveland is one of the most improved forces in England and Wales, with performance levels also judged to be some of the best in the country.

The force has recently arrested 87 people for offences linked to organised crime gangs and over the past two years 16 people have been jailed for such crimes.

Fuller denied that gangs had control over parts of Middlesbrough, describing it as a "complex" area to police, with high rates of school absence, drug addiction and mental health issues.

"We're doing the very, very best with what we've got - and we absolutely do need more."

Authorities say high deprivation and unemployment in the area are fuelling organised crime.

"When young people have little aspiration or hope, who don't have confidence in the state, then unfortunately criminals exploit these people," Fuller said.

"They give confidence, and they give them hope, and they give them aspiration. And sadly what that means is young people doing things without thought of consequences."

GeneralTab.title: Why are European countries moving their gold out of North America?
GeneralTab.text:
When the central bank of the Netherlands confirmed this week that it had moved tonnes of the country's gold out of North America, it said the relocation would make it "better prepared for severe crises".

Some 86 tonnes from the combined total of about 313 tonnes held in the US and Canada were relocated to London "in view of increasing geopolitical unrest", it said, so the shiny stuff could be "readily available for use in a crisis situation".

Questions were bound to follow. Why were the Dutch doing this? Were they anticipating some major economic shock on the horizon?

It seems not, but the move was clearly in response to the unstable and uncertain state the world finds itself in, with trade and military wars prompting countries to take precautions and hold their gold closer to home.

Earlier this year, France announced it had removed its gold reserves from the US to home shores. Meanwhile, Germany's Bundesbank transferred more than 216 tonnes of the metal from storage locations abroad - 111 tonnes from New York and 105 tonnes from Paris - over a few years ending in 2016., external

It is a strategy which has played out before in times of global instability. "Some European central banks moved part of their gold holdings to New York during the Cold War," said research analysts Lina Thomas and Daan Struyven of Goldman Sachs.

Joseph Cavatoni, senior market strategist at the World Gold Council, told the BBC while wars and trade tensions were "playing into some of these decisions", it didn't "top the list" of motivating factors.

Inflation, interest rates and just having gold in a place where it can be traded quickly also played a role.

"I don't get a sense that there's an impending doom," Cavatoni said, "but what I do think is people are being better educated around how to manage their reserve assets, growing their reserve assets, and actually thinking more effectively around how to make the most of those assets."

De Nederlandsche Bank said the gold removed from the US and Canada between March and August this year was now being held in the vaults of the Bank of England.

"We expect that we will never need to use them, but we do need to strengthen our resilience and preparedness," said the governor of the Dutch central bank, Olaf Sleijpen.

London was seen as the best choice due its position in the world as a major trading centre. If you want to be able to buy or sell gold fast in a crisis, London is the place to be, which makes the Bank of England a popular storage spot.

The Bank is one of the largest custodians of gold in the world. Underneath the 300-year-old institution in central London sit about 400,000 bars worth more than £200bn.

According to industry surveys by the World Gold Council, the Bank of England remains the most popular vaulting location, but central banks are increasingly diversifying where they store the precious metal.

Where to store your country's gold is "increasingly top of mind for reserve managers", according to Thomas and Struyven of Goldman Sachs.

In the modern world, there are many ways to shift your treasure around. The Dutch sold about 59 tonnes in New York and then bought more stocks in London, meaning that amount didn't need to be hauled across the Atlantic.

But more than 27 tonnes were "physically transferred" from the US and Canada to the Dutch town of Zeist. A similar quantity was also sent from Zeist to London.

Companies that perform such services are tight-lipped on how operations are carried out, but it's fair to say the security measures and planning are extensive to avoid the risk of a real-life Italian Job.

Cavatoni, of the World Gold Council, said one standard approach to move gold stocks was to sell the commodity in one place and buy it in another. "Let's say I want my gold in New York and I have it in London. I could sell it in London, buy it in New York, same day, same time, effectively book transfer without actually having to put it on any other logistical change."

There are only a few select companies which handle gold shipments across borders, one of which is Brink's Global Services, who told the BBC it had seen "increased demand" from the likes of central banks in recent times.

"Heightened geopolitical and economic uncertainty, along with gold's growing role as a strategic reserve asset, appear to be contributing to this trend," said Nader Antar, Brink's executive vice president.

GeneralTab.title: Trump calls for interest rate cut after jobs figures raise hike bets
GeneralTab.text:
Donald Trump has called for interest rates to be cut later this month, claiming higher rates put the US at a "very unfair disadvantage".

The president's remarks came as stronger-than-expected jobs figures in the US added to growing expectations that rates could be increased, with inflation still running high and American households feeling the pinch of rising prices.

The number of roles added to the economy increased by 162,000 in August, almost triple the 56,000 forecast by analysts, driven by a boost in hospitality and education hiring.

Trump said the US should have the "LOWEST RATE of any country in the World".

"The Fed Board, with its great new leader, must get smart - BE PATRIOTS for a change. High interest rates put the U.S.A. at a very unfair disadvantage, and I won't allow that to happen!", the president said in a post on social media, external.

Last week, Kevin Warsh, chairman of the US central bank, signalled that rates could be hiked if policymakers were not confident price rises were easing for Americans.

Inflation, which measures price increases over time, remains above the Fed's 2% annual target, with prices up 3.4% in the past 12 months, according to the latest data.

The next interest rate decision will be made on 15-16 September. Rates were left unchanged between 3.5% and 3.75% in July for the fifth time in a row, but concerns over inflation remain due to the ongoing conflict between the US and Iran, which has caused as surge in global oil prices.

On Friday, US diesel prices hit an all-time high of $5.85 a gallon on average, compared to $3.71 a year ago.

But despite the cost of living rising, wages also appear to be increasing. In August, average hourly earnings for all employees were $37.75 on average, having increased 3.1%.

"Even the most committed dove would struggle to find anything in the August employment report to justify keeping interest rates unchanged," said Stephen Brown, chief North America economist at Capital Economics.

He added that the strength in the jobs market meant that the latest inflation figures released next week would only need to be moderately above the Fed's target to fuel expectations of a September hike.

"A hike in rates just became a bit more likely," said Neil Birrell, chief investment office of investment firm Premier Miton.

Almost 60% of traders were betting on an interest rate hike in September, according to CME Group's "FedWatch" data.

An increase in employment during the final month of the summer in restaurants and bars, as well as in local government education ahead of the new school year, was behind August's labour market rebound.

Weaker job figures released earlier in the summer were revised up by the US Bureau of Labor Statistics, revealing a stronger labour market than previously thought. Instead of the economy being deemed to have shed 23,000 jobs in July, some 44,000 were found to have been created in subsequent estimates.

While many more jobs were added, the US unemployment rate remained unchanged at 4.1% last month, with seven million out of work. Both measures have changed little over the year.

In response to the stronger jobs figures raising expectations of a interest rate hike, US stock market indexes were trading down on Friday.

Trump called the response "crazy". "We just got GREAT Numbers on Jobs, the Market should go UP, because our Credit and Economy are better but, as always, for the past 25 years, the Stock Market goes DOWN, because we're living under False Reality that if things are good, you've got to "KILL IT" because of a "fear" of Inflation," he said.

articles.title: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' in foreign donor talks
articles.text:
Nigel Farage has said he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what appears to have been a scheme to funnel foreign money to Reform UK.

His former chief of staff Dan Jukes and ex-head of policy James Orr have both been removed from their jobs after an investigation recorded them talking about how to get money to the party from an American donor and asking a fake company to pay for polling.

Jukes has denied doing anything wrong. Orr has told Sky News he will co-operate fully with Reform's internal investigation.

In an interview with the BBC, the Reform leader said he was not listening to the discussion and revealed his family are "begging" him to leave his job amid increasing pressure.

In a film by Verbatim Investigations and Channel 4 News, Farage and Jukes were present during a conversation in which it is suggested the US donor gives £500,000 to Reform through his UK-based son.

Under electoral law, donors to UK political parties must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK, so cannot give money from abroad through a British resident.

The proposed donation was never made as it was part of an undercover sting, but that it was seemingly entertained has sparked questions.

When asked about the exchange by reporters at Reform's party conference on Friday, Farage said he was questioning whether the arrangement was above board.

In an interview to be broadcast on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, he has now said: "I am not a compliance officer. I was in the middle of canvassing in the Clacton by-election. I turn up. I frankly wasn't even listening."

"I was told there was a global family office based in London, so the money could have come from Singapore," he said of the conversation in the Channel 4 film.

"The money could come from all over the world, you know. Income could have came from all over the world into a family office based in London. I know electoral law. I know donation law better than anybody.

"Frankly, the two individuals involved here have never been involved in fundraising before and they shouldn't have been involved directly in fundraising. They should have done basic checks and nobody, nobody should be brought to me, unless they've been vetted from."

The row over the Channel 4 film has threatened to capsize Reform's conference, with Labour and the Liberal Democrats calling on the Metropolitan Police to investigate the claims. The force is assessing whether or not to investigate.

Jukes and Orr - both senior figures in Farage's inner circle - have stood down pending the outcome of the party's internal investigation, but political opponents are demanding that Farage is investigated and takes accountability.

Farage categorically denied that Reform had ever taken money from a foreign entity by channelling it through a UK donor.

But as pressure ramps up on Farage in the latest crisis to rock Reform, he also told the BBC that "for the first time", he does not have his family's support to be in politics.

"They would rather I packed it up and walked away," he said.

He added he had not considered standing down, but "when you've got your family begging you to, it's not easy".

Farage also condemned the hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters who descended on the Port of Dover on Saturday morning, causing major travel disruption.

Farage said he "deplored" anyone wearing masks or balaclavas at public demonstrations.

He added: "You should not be allowed to be masked up, balaclava-ed up and go out and protest on the streets of our country. It is wrong at every level. So I deplore what is happening in Dover today."

There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election.

Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days".

They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats.

They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029.

They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest.

Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage.

But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money.

What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump.

At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake.

One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions".

No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty".

And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base.

Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved.

A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up – sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage".

Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said.

But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera – Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say."

But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?"

This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing.

Farage's admission that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling – to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on.

articles.title: Reform UK winded by donations row as insiders call for shift in approach
articles.text:
"We are still a bit of a pirate ship," a senior Reform figure acknowledges privately.

It was the recurring conversation throughout Reform UK's conference in Birmingham: the consequences of the undercover filming broadcast by Channel 4 News which has cost two senior party figures their jobs, at least for now.

How much damage does it cause to Reform? And what does it tell us about them?

"A key part of the appeal of us is the sense of us being cavaliers. Doing things differently. Standing out. And that's great. But we need roundheads too. Those who ask the boring questions. Do the checks. We need more of them too," this same senior figure adds.

The story of Reform over the last 12 months can be summarised in three words: defections, elections and money.

Defections, those who leave one party and join another, have been a big part of the party's growth in the last year – not least the recruitment of former Conservative cabinet ministers Robert Jenrick and Suella Braverman.

Elections have been as well - Reform's gains in the English local elections and the devolved parliament elections in Wales and in Scotland.

But so too has money. The backdrop to this conference was the swirl of questions about money even before Channel 4 News', and Verbatim Investigations', endeavours.

In the hour or two before its broadcast on Thursday night, senior Reform figures, including those directly caught up in it, projected a sense of being relatively relaxed about it. Awkward, embarrassing, but survivable.

Once it was broadcast, things changed. There was fury, I am told, and very quickly there was a sense of its gravity. "A few bottles of red were had, and we knew we had to act," is how one source described it to me. The conversations went on into the early hours.

Firstly, there was anger that it would drown out a conference that has been months in the planning. And yes, it has dominated conversation here in Birmingham.

Secondly, there was widespread concern about the image it projected, the impression it would leave.

Reform wants to project itself as a prospective party of government.

And yet the headlines allow critics to claim they are not just ramshackle and amateurish but can point to what looks like a pattern of activity, consciously pursued, to breach the law.

Absolutely not, Nigel Farage insisted to me, there was no such pattern.

But what of the ethos of the party? Journalist Tim Shipman in The Spectator writes , externalthat "it is the experience of everyone I have ever known near the summit of politics that political operations take their character and operating logic from the person at the apex of the triangle. Leaders set culture."

There is something in this. Take Rishi Sunak's Downing Street operation and Boris Johnson's. They were wildly different culturally, reflecting the very different characters at their helm. Would all the things that happened during Partygate under Johnson have happened under Sunak? Unlikely, I would have thought.

Some within Reform, who are full of admiration for Nigel Farage's chutzpah and gift as a communicator, are desperate to see a behind-the-scenes cultural shift that minimises the chances of further embarrassments. And, alongside that, a step up in the infrastructure and personnel to match.

Farage's team express frustration that this is precisely what they have been doing, but some are telling them internally they need to move more quickly.

Both James Orr, the party's head of policy; and Dan Jukes, Farage's right-hand man, will be missed profoundly by those inside the party.

Privately, some wonder if Orr may yet return.

Jukes, who has been a pivotal and loyal figure in Team Farage for years, was already dividing his time between the UK and the United States as his wife and baby are on the other side of the Atlantic.

Perhaps, some senior figures suggest, his immediate future might be in America. Does he return when the general election is nearer? Let's see.

Reform leave Birmingham winded and wounded by the last few days, their days in the sun overshadowed.

The question is how they deal with this and respond to it, in the coming weeks and months.

articles.title: Cleveland police chief proud of force but being 'let down' by funding
articles.text:
Cleveland Police's Chief Constable has said she is proud of her "brave" force but that it was being "let down" by the way it was funded, following a fatal crash which killed seven people including two police officers.

In her first sit-down interview since the A66 crash, speaking exclusively to the BBC, Victoria Fuller said the force needed to become part of a larger force with greater resources.

She said her officers are dealing with some of the highest crime levels in the country akin to those faced by metropolitan forces, but with less than half the number of officers.

Multiple people have since been arrested as part of a wider police operation against organised crime following the crash.

A Volkswagen Passat carrying five young men drove the wrong way down the motorway near Middlesbrough in the early hours of the morning before colliding with a marked police car.

Officers had been pursuing the car for almost seven minutes after it was connected to earlier alleged criminal activity, but the pursuit was abandoned 10 seconds before the crash when the Passat turned on to the dual carriageway, the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) said.

Fuller, whose force covers an area of north-east England that includes Middlesbrough and Teesside, recalled being asleep when the duty commander rang her with the news.

"No matter how tragic and devastated you feel, we swing into action and we do what we need to do," she said.

The home secretary announced this week that Cleveland Police would be given an extra £2m to deal with the fallout from the crash, with 200 officers drafted in from elsewhere.

Fuller told the BBC on Friday that she was grateful for the support the force had been given, but added: "I need that all the time."

Cleveland's Labour police and crime commissioner has previously said the force needed an extra £20m a year to hire more officers and crack down on organised crime.

Cleveland Police is grappling with the highest recorded crime rate of anywhere in England and Wales, Office for National Statistics (ONS) figures for the year to March show.

It also ranks highest for burglary, sexual offences, violence with injury, and criminal damage and arson.

Fuller said Cleveland Police had also experienced the largest decrease in the number of officers since 2010 and was staffed as if it were a rural force.

"It absolutely needs to change," she said.

Fuller expressed hope that reform to policing across the country was on the horizon, and that Cleveland Police would become one of the "big, strategic forces that have the resource, the flex and the capability to surge when they need to surge".

She added: "In the meantime, we need additional funding... to take us to that point."

Recent inspections show Cleveland is one of the most improved forces in England and Wales, with performance levels also judged to be some of the best in the country.

The force has recently arrested 87 people for offences linked to organised crime gangs and over the past two years 16 people have been jailed for such crimes.

Fuller denied that gangs had control over parts of Middlesbrough, describing it as a "complex" area to police, with high rates of school absence, drug addiction and mental health issues.

"We're doing the very, very best with what we've got - and we absolutely do need more."

Authorities say high deprivation and unemployment in the area are fuelling organised crime.

"When young people have little aspiration or hope, who don't have confidence in the state, then unfortunately criminals exploit these people," Fuller said.

"They give confidence, and they give them hope, and they give them aspiration. And sadly what that means is young people doing things without thought of consequences."

articles.title: Michael Owen doesn't tell his children he loves them - how big a deal is that?
articles.text:
England football legend Michael Owen sparked debate this week after saying he "never ever" tells his children he loves them - despite them being "the most dearest things in the world" to him.

"I don't say anything like that," the father-of-four told Jamie Laing in a podcast interview., external "I just assume my actions would show them that I love them. I think most of us are like that."

While some were surprised at Owen's comments, saying they always make sure to tell their children how they feel, other parents say they share the ex-striker's outlook.

The exchange has highlighted different attitudes around parenting, gender and culture, and raises the question - just how important are those three simple words?

Experts tell us making your child feel loved comes from more than just a simple turn of phrase.

Educational psychologist Dr Patricia Britto says while words can often be crucial, the most important thing is that a child feels "safe, valued and emotionally secure".

"We shouldn't conclude that children have been psychologically damaged and harmed simply because they don't hear those words," she tells the BBC. "They may experience love very clearly through actions."

Dr Britto says the bigger issue for many children is whether they feel affection is "consistently communicated" which can come through both words and actions, or better yet a combination of the two.

"If you said to a child 'I love you, I love you' but you never turn up to any of their football games or shows, they might not actually feel loved. They might just feel they are empty words."

Dad Aaron Dale, host of the Raisingboys2men podcast and author of a book on parenting, agrees.

"It's not words or actions - they shouldn't compete against each other, they should complement each other.

"Words are to speak the message and actions are the evidence."

Dale pointed to how his own father would often tell him "I love you" after letting him down, diminishing the meaning of the words.

However, some parents believe it is absolutely crucial their child hears that they are loved.

One father of a seven-year-old daughter, told us he was surprised by Owen's comments, describing them as "awful".

"You should always tell your children you love them no matter what, when they're bad, when they're good," he said.

And reacting online to the clip of Owen, another parent wrote: "Parents and potential parents do not listen to this man. Tell your kids you love them everyday, even when it annoys them."

To the outside observer, Owen's love for his children is not in doubt.

The trailer for his new show, Meet the Owens, shows glimpses of what appears to be a happy home life with his wife and children. And in 2024, the former England striker spoke movingly about his son James's sight loss, saying: "If I could give him my eyes... I would."

Pushed by podcast host Laing to explain why he doesn't let the 'I love yous' flow freely, Owen told Laing that "I would love to be a little bit soft".

"I'm definitely getting softer," he said, "but still not soft enough to say anything like that."

Using the word "soft" to describe telling your children you love them reflects long-standing attitudes many fathers have towards parenting, both Dale and Dr Britto suggest.

They say it's a result of different contexts, such as culture, class, gender and a generational divide

"I think that's the dangerous part there," Dale says, "the belief of what men should and what men shouldn't do."

Many fathers believe their role is simply to "provide", but they can do so much more, he says.

"Men are much more than just providers... what about our emotional capacity and willingness to have conversations and be there as fathers? And maybe we can't provide, but you know what? Our presence is at full capacity."

He adds that he thinks people's style of parenting "always stems from somewhere", including whether they were often told they were loved as a child.

Gender expectations and masculinity are not the only element at play, Dr Britto says.

"In some cultures they don't even use those words [I love you] at all," she says. "They may ask things like 'Have you eaten?' as a sign of love rather than actually saying 'I love you'."

She adds: "As an African myself, in Nigerian culture parents don't always say 'I love you'... but I still felt loved."

Parents also suggest that different generations may approach showing love for their children in different ways.

Reacting on social media, one says Owen is right to suggest actions speak louder than words: "My dad never said the words, but it was also never in doubt."

Another writes: "What's the big deal? My dad - and I'm sure most dads of our generation - didn't. He did something far, far better than emotional words he 'showed us' by his actions."

While Owen's comments may have triggered strong feelings, it is clear there are countless ways parents communicate love to their children.

Above all, says Dr Britto, it's about making sure children feel a sense of belonging. "Do they feel loved?" she says. "Do they feel wanted?

"Do they feel that they matter, rather than simply hearing the words?"
